title: Concept Drills — Fundamentals of Applied Chemistry (Class 11 Chemistry)
subject: chemistry

questions.question: Why does a bag of NPK fertiliser list three numbers, and what does each supply to the plant?
questions.solution: The numbers give the percentage of N, P₂O₅ and K₂O — the three nutrients plants consume most: N for leaf/protein growth, P for roots and energy transfer (ATP), K for water regulation and disease resistance. Fertiliser chemistry is targeted ion supply, not generic 'food'.

questions.question: Why does cement SET when water is added — what reaction is occurring, and why is the process not simply 'drying'?
questions.solution: Clinker minerals (especially calcium silicates) HYDRATE: water reacts chemically with them, forming interlocking hydrated silicate crystals — the setting is a chemical bonding process, not evaporation. That is why cement cures even underwater, and why keeping it moist during curing strengthens it.

questions.question: Why is glass called a supercooled liquid rather than a true solid, and what practical property shows this?
questions.solution: Glass lacks the ordered lattice of crystals: on cooling, its molecules freeze in a disordered arrangement without crystallising. Evidence: glass has no sharp melting point (it softens gradually) and very old glass shows flow (thicker at the bottom). Amorphous structure = gradual softening, no fixed melting point.

questions.question: Distinguish addition and condensation polymerisation with one example each.
questions.solution: Addition: monomers with C=C simply add to each other, nothing is eliminated (ethylene → polyethene). Condensation: monomers join with the ELIMINATION of a small molecule (usually water) — e.g. nylon from diamine + dicarboxylic acid. Addition keeps all atoms; condensation loses some — that is why condensation polymers (nylon, polyester) have ester/amide links in the backbone.

questions.question: How does one soap molecule clean both grease and water? Describe the two ends and the micelle.
questions.solution: Soap = R–COO⁻Na⁺: a hydrocarbon tail (dissolves in grease, non-polar) and a carboxylate head (dissolves in water, polar). Molecules surround grease droplets tails-in, heads-out — a MICELLE — so the whole droplet becomes water-dispersible and rinses away. Amphiphilic structure is the cleaning mechanism.
